subject: math
title: Properties of Multiplication
seo_title: Grade 3 Properties of Multiplication Worksheets: Commutative, Associative and Distributive (with Arrays)
standard_text: Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide. Examples: If 6 × 4 = 24 is known, then 4 × 6 = 24 is also known. (Commutative property of multiplication.) 3 × 5 × 2 can be found by 3 × 5 = 15, then 15 × 2 = 30, or by 5 × 2 = 10, then 3 × 10 = 30. (Associative property of multiplication.) Knowing that 8 × 5 = 40 and 8 × 2 = 16, one can find 8 × 7 as 8 × (5 + 2) = (8 × 5) + (8 × 2) = 40 + 16 = 56. (Distributive property.)
meta_desc: Free Grade 3 properties of multiplication worksheets: commutative, associative and distributive properties with arrays, plus times 1 and times 0. Split arrays, missing numbers and word problems. 100 practice questions with answers.
key_big: Change the order or the grouping, and the product stays the same. Split a hard fact into two easy ones.
body_html:
Why the properties help

The properties of multiplication are rules that work for every number. They let you turn a fact you do not know into facts you already know.

Commutative property: change the order

Switch the factors and the product stays the same. Turn an array on its side: the dots do not change.

If you know 6 × 4 = 24, you also know 4 × 6 = 24.

Identity and zero properties

PropertyRuleExample
Identity property of multiplicationA number × 1 = the same number9 × 1 = 9
Zero property of multiplicationA number × 0 = 09 × 0 = 0

Associative property: change the grouping

With three factors, you may multiply any two first. Look for a pair that makes 10.

Example

Find 3 × 5 × 2.

(3 × 5) × 2 = 15 × 2 = 30, or 3 × (5 × 2) = 3 × 10 = 30.

Answer: 30

Distributive property: split the array

Split one factor into two easier parts. Multiply each part, then add the two products.

Example

You know 6 × 5 = 30. Find 6 × 9.

9 = 5 + 4. (6 × 5) + (6 × 4) = 30 + 24 = 54.

Answer: 54

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
8 × 7 = (8 × 5) + 2Multiply both parts: (8 × 5) + (8 × 2) = 56
Splitting 7 into 4 + 2The parts must add up to the factor: 5 + 2 = 7
9 × 0 = 9Times 0 is always 0. Times 1 keeps the number
9 − 4 = 4 − 9Switching the order works for × and +, not for − or ÷
Mixing up commutative and associativeCommutative: the order changes. Associative: the parentheses move

faq.q: What is the distributive property in 3rd grade?
faq.a: It means you can split one factor into two parts, multiply each part, and add the products. For example, 8 × 7 = (8 × 5) + (8 × 2) = 40 + 16 = 56.

faq.q: What is the commutative property of multiplication?
faq.a: Changing the order of the factors does not change the product: 6 × 4 = 4 × 6 = 24. Each fact you learn gives you its turn-around fact for free.

faq.q: What is the difference between the commutative and associative properties?
faq.a: The commutative property changes the order of the factors (3 × 5 = 5 × 3). The associative property keeps the order and changes the grouping: (2 × 7) × 5 = 2 × (7 × 5).

faq.q: Do 3rd graders need to know the names of the properties?
faq.a: The Common Core standard 3.OA.B.5 says students do not need to use the formal names; they need to use the properties as strategies. Many teachers and tests still use the names, so learning them helps.

items.e: 2 × 5 = 10, and 10 × 8 = 80 is easy. The other groupings with × give the same product, but with harder steps. (2 + 5) × 8 adds instead of multiplying.

sets.title: Name the property and solve word problems

items.q:
Which property does this equation show?
4 × 7 = 7 × 4
items.e: This is the commutative property. The factors switch places, and the product stays the same.

items.q:
Which property does this equation show?
(2 × 3) × 4 = 2 × (3 × 4)
items.e: This is the associative property. The factors stay in the same order. Only the parentheses move, which changes what you multiply first.

items.q:
Which property does this equation show?
6 × (5 + 2) = (6 × 5) + (6 × 2)
items.e: This is the distributive property. One factor is split into two parts. Each part is multiplied, and the products are added.

items.q:
Which property does this equation show?
9 × 1 = 9
items.e: This is the identity property of multiplication. Multiplying by 1 keeps the number the same.

items.q:
Which property does this equation show?
0 × 8 = 0
items.e: This is the zero property of multiplication. Multiplying by 0 always gives 0.

items.q:
Which property does this equation show?
(4 × 5) + (4 × 3) = 4 × 8
items.e: This is the distributive property. One factor is split into two parts. Each part is multiplied, and the products are added.

items.q: Which equation shows the commutative property?
items.e: Commutative means the order changes: 3 × 8 and 8 × 3 have the same factors in a different order.

items.q: Which equation shows the distributive property?
items.e: 6 is split into 5 + 1. Each part is multiplied by 7, and the two products are added: 35 + 7 = 42.

items.q: Maya sets up 6 rows of 8 chairs. Leo sets up 8 rows of 6 chairs. Who sets up more chairs?
items.e: 6 × 8 = 48 and 8 × 6 = 48, so they set up the same number. Switching the order does not change the product. (14 comes from adding 6 + 8.)

items.q: A box has 4 rows of 9 crayons. Ava says the total is 4 × 9. Ben says it is 9 × 4. Who is right?
items.e: 4 rows of 9 can also be read as 9 columns of 4. 4 × 9 = 9 × 4 = 36.

items.q: Each of 9 students gets 1 library card. How many library cards are given out?
items.e: 9 groups of 1: 9 × 1 = 9 cards.

items.q: Omar has 5 boxes. Each box has 0 marbles left in it. How many marbles are in the boxes?
items.e: 5 groups of 0: 5 × 0 = 0 marbles.

items.q: A muffin tray has 3 rows of 4 cups. A baker fills 2 trays. How many muffins does the baker make?
items.e: 3 × 4 × 2. One tray is 3 × 4 = 12, and 2 trays are 12 × 2 = 24. Or group 4 × 2 = 8 first: 3 × 8 = 24.

items.q: An egg carton has 2 rows of 6 eggs. How many eggs are in 5 cartons?
items.e: 2 × 6 × 5. Group 2 × 5 = 10 first, then 10 × 6 = 60 eggs.

items.q: There are 2 tables. Each table has 5 students. Each student has 8 crayons. How many crayons are there in all?
items.e: 2 × 5 × 8. Group 2 × 5 = 10 students first, then 10 × 8 = 80 crayons.

items.q: A wall has 7 rows of 3 tiles. Another wall has the same number of tiles in 3 rows. How many tiles are in each row of the second wall?
items.e: 7 × 3 = 21 tiles. 3 rows of 7 is also 21, because 3 × 7 = 7 × 3.

items.q: Kai plants 6 rows of 7 tomato plants. He knows that 6 × 5 = 30. How can he find 6 × 7?
items.e: 7 = 5 + 2, so 6 × 7 = (6 × 5) + (6 × 2) = 30 + 12 = 42. The extra 2 columns have 6 plants each.

items.q: Mia knows that 7 × 5 = 35. How can she find 7 × 6?
items.e: 7 × 6 is one more group of 7 than 7 × 5: (7 × 5) + (7 × 1) = 35 + 7 = 42.

items.q: Noah buys 4 packs of markers with 8 markers in each pack. He splits 8 into 5 + 3. How many markers does he buy?
items.e: 4 × 8 = (4 × 5) + (4 × 3) = 20 + 12 = 32 markers. Both parts are multiplied by 4.

items.q: Lily knows that 10 × 8 = 80. A sheet has 9 rows of 8 stickers. How many stickers are on the sheet?
items.e: 9 rows is 1 row fewer than 10 rows. Take away one row of 8: 80 − 8 = 72 stickers.
